segments.translit: jñānapānapramatto hi siddhācāryyamahīdharaḥ | cittagajendrasandhyayā tam ekārtha pratipādayati —
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Mahīdhara]{p-mahidhara}, [drunk]{matta} on the drink of knowledge, sets forth that same meaning in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of 'the [mind]{citta}, lord of [elephants]{elephant}':
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the poet: the [siddha]{siddha} master [Mahīdhara]{p-mahidhara}, [drunk]{matta} on the drink of knowledge, teaches in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of 'the [mind]{citta}, lord of [elephants]{elephant}' (cp.16.m1). The song's elephant is, for him, the mind.

equations.en: the mind, as lord of elephants

flags.note: Shastri prints tamekārtha. As it stands this is tam ekārtha[ṃ], 'that single (or same) meaning', lacking the anusvāra. It may be a slip for tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning', Munidatta's usual phrase (cp.16.m4 has tam evārtha[ṃ] dyotayati); ক and ব are easily confused. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', but it also renders tam evārthaṃ in cp.16.m4 by de kho na nyid, so it probably read tam eva here too. I translate 'that same meaning', which suits either reading.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) puts Mahīdhara in the genitive, 'the mind itself of the siddha master Sa 'dzin, lord of elephants' (sa 'dzin gyi thugs nyid glang po che'i dbang po), and ends with a purpose clause, 'in order to make the meaning of reality understood' (de kho na nyid kyi don rtogs par bya ba'i phyir). It renders sandhyā by dgongs pa'i skad, 'intentional language'.

cittagajendra is the Sanskrit of the refrain's own word cīagaandā (cīa, 'mind', with gaanda, 'lord of elephants'; cp.16.2a), which the Tibetan line renders sems nyid … glang chen dbang po, 'the mind itself … lord of elephants'. The current draft of 2a has only 'elephant'; see questions.

segments.translit:
pāṭatrayaṃ kāyānandādikaṃ tam abhedopacāreṇa gṛhītvā jñānapānamadireṇa lagnaḥ | tathā ca kāyaṃ kāyākāreṇa cittaṃ cittākāreṇa kāyaṃ cittaṃ vākpratyāhāreṇa ity uktaṃ | guhyasamāje | tatrasthajñānamadhupānena pramattasiddhācāryyamahīdharasya cittagajendraḥ | anāhatam iti śūnyatāśabdaṃ | kasaṇa bhayānakaṃ | śūnyatānādaṃ śrutvā kaṇṭhagarjjanaṃ karoti | tam anāhataṃ śabdaṃ śrutvā saṃsārabhayaṅkarāgantukaskandhakleśādayo mārā bhagnāḥ |
tathā ca rativajre —
mantraprayogamaṇḍalaṃ yena bhagnaṃ mahābalaṃ |
mārasainyaṃ mahāghoraṃ śākyasiṃhādibhir buddhaiḥ ||
segments.translation: The three [pāṭa]{pata}s are the [joy]{ananda} of the body and the rest. Taking them, figuratively, as non-different, he is attached through the intoxication of the drink of knowledge. And so it is said in the [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}: 'the body in the form of the body, the [mind]{citta} in the form of the mind, body and mind by the withdrawal of speech.' The mind, lord of [elephants]{elephant}, of the [siddha]{siddha} master [Mahīdhara]{p-mahidhara}, [drunk]{matta} on drinking the honey-liquor of knowledge found there. '[Unstruck]{anahata}' means the sound of [emptiness]{sunyata}. 'Kasaṇa' means terrifying. Hearing the sound of emptiness, it roars from its throat. Hearing that unstruck sound, the [Māras]{mara} that make [saṃsāra]{samsara} fearful, the adventitious [aggregates]{skandha}, [afflictions]{klesa} and the rest, are broken. And so in the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra}: 'The [maṇḍala]{mandala} of mantra practice, by which the [buddhas]{buddha}, [Śākyasiṃha]{p-sakyasimha} and the rest, broke [Māra]{mara}'s army, mighty and most dreadful.'
segments.note: Munidatta takes the three [pāṭa]{pata}s as the [joys]{ananda} beginning with the joy of the body, taken as non-different (cp.16.m2). In his reading it is Mahīdhara's mind-elephant, drunk on knowledge, that roars on hearing the [unstruck]{anahata} sound, the sound of emptiness; and the [Māras]{mara}, the adventitious aggregates, afflictions and the rest, are broken.

equations.en: the joys beginning with the joy of the body (kāyānanda)
the adventitious aggregates, afflictions and the rest, which make saṃsāra fearful

citations.quoted: kāyaṃ kāyākāreṇa cittaṃ cittākāreṇa kāyaṃ cittaṃ vākpratyāhāreṇa
mantraprayogamaṇḍalaṃ yena bhagnaṃ mahābalaṃ | mārasainyaṃ mahāghoraṃ śākyasiṃhādibhir buddhaiḥ

flags.note: In the draft of 1a the unstruck sound itself roars. Munidatta makes the mind-elephant the one that roars: hearing the sound of emptiness, 'it roars from its throat' (kaṇṭhagarjanaṃ karoti), the subject being the cittagajendra named just before. He does not gloss ghaṇa, 'deep'; at that point the Tibetan line has an elephant: rab 'jigs glang chen sgrogs, 'the most terrifying elephant roars'. I have not harmonized song and commentary; see questions.

The Guhyasamāja passage reads oddly as printed (kāyaṃ kāyākāreṇa cittaṃ cittākāreṇa kāyaṃ cittaṃ vākpratyāhāreṇa). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has it crosswise: 'by the aspect of body, to the mind; by the aspect of mind, to the body; from the mind, by speech, it is uttered' (sku'i rnam pas thugs la thugs kyi rnam pas sku la/ thugs las gsung gis rab tu brjod par). That suggests kāyaṃ cittākāreṇa cittaṃ kāyākāreṇa … vākpravyāhāreṇa, since rab tu brjod pa renders pravyāhāra, 'utterance', not pratyāhāra, 'withdrawal'. I translate the printed Sanskrit and have not been able to check the tantra itself.

Smaller differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): 'intoxication by the drink of wisdom is attained' (myos pa ni thob pa'o) for 'he is attached through the intoxication' (madireṇa lagnaḥ); 'from that place' (de'i gnas las) for 'found there' (tatrastha); 'greatly delighted' (rab tu dgyes pa) for 'drunk' (pramatta); the gloss of kasaṇa is joined to the next sentence ('very terrifying and frightening' means: hearing the tone of emptiness, it roars in the throat); and the sound actively destroys the Māras ('joms par byed pa) where the Sanskrit has them broken.

In the Rativajra verse the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'the incomparable application of secret mantra' (gsang sngags sbyor ba mnyam med pa), with nothing for maṇḍala, and 'the wise' (mkhas rnams) where the Sanskrit has 'buddhas' (buddhaiḥ), perhaps reading budhaiḥ.

As quoted, the Rativajra verse has no main verb: the maṇḍala of mantra practice heads a relative clause, so the quotation may be an excerpt. In the song it is Māra's own maṇḍala that breaks; in the verse the maṇḍala is the means by which Māra's army was broken. Munidatta does not comment on the song's saa maṇḍala. Also, lagnaḥ has no expressed subject: 'he' may be Mahīdhara or his mind-elephant; tatrastha, 'found there', presumably points to the three joys.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tasya nirbharānandapramodaṃ prakaṭayati —
mātela ityādi | sa eva pramatto hi cittagajendraś candrasūryyadivārātrivikalpaṃ gholayitvā gaganopadeśacaturthānandopadeśaṃ gṛhītvā gacchatīti mahāsukhasarasi nirantaraṃ |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes plain his delight in full [joy]{ananda}: '[Drunk]{matta}…' and so on. That same [mind]{citta}, lord of [elephants]{elephant}, drunk as it is, churns up the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of [moon]{moon} and [sun]{surya}, of day and night, takes the [instruction]{upadesa} of the [sky]{gagana}, the instruction of the fourth joy, and goes, without pause, in the [lake]{lake} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
segments.note: Munidatta hears in the [refrain]{dhruvapada} the delight of full [joy]{ananda} (cp.16.m3). The drunk mind-elephant churns up the concepts of moon and sun, day and night, takes the instruction of the [sky]{gagana}, the instruction of the fourth joy, and goes without pause in the lake of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.

equations.en: the instruction of the fourth joy (caturthānandopadeśa), in apposition

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'because it is drunk on reality, the mind is the lord of elephants' (de kho na nyid kyis myos pa'i phyir sems ni glang po che'i dbang po'o) where the Sanskrit has 'that same mind, lord of elephants, drunk as it is' (sa eva pramatto hi cittagajendraḥ); de kho na can render eva, 'just that', so this may be the translators' construal rather than a different reading. It has 'having destroyed' (bshig nas) for 'having churned' (gholayitvā), and makes the running itself 'the unceasing lake of great bliss' (rgyug par byed pa ni bde ba chen po'i rdzing bu rgyun mi 'chad pa'o).

mahāsukhasarasi nirantaraṃ stands after gacchatīti with no verb of its own; I take it with 'goes'. It may gloss the song's nirantara gaaṇanta, putting the lake of great bliss where the song has the edge of the sky, but Munidatta does not say so. tasya, 'his', may refer to Mahīdhara or to the mind-elephant.

Munidatta makes the object of the song's gholai 'the conceptual thought of moon and sun, of day and night'; the draft of 2b has the elephant churn the edge of the sky. The Tibetan line of 2b has sun and moon circling in the sky (nam mkha'i phyogs su nyi zla 'khor).

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tam evārtha[ṃ] dyotayati —
pāpa puṇyetyādi | pāpapuṇyau saṃsārapāśau dvau khaṇḍayitvā | khambheti avidyāstambhaṃ marddayitvā | gaganaṭaketi anāhataśabdena preritaḥ san sa eva cittagajendro nirvvāṇasarovaraṃ gataḥ |
tathā ca kṛṣṇācāryyāḥ —
khiti jaletyādi |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he brings out that same meaning: '[Sin and merit]{papa-punya}…' and so on. Cutting the two, sin and merit, the two [nooses]{noose} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. '[Pillar]{khambha}' means crushing the pillar of [ignorance]{avidya}. 'Gagana[ṭaka]{takali}' means that, driven on by the [unstruck]{anahata} sound, that same [mind]{citta}, lord of [elephants]{elephant}, went to the [lake]{lake} of [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}. And so [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}: 'Earth, water…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the second verse as the mind-elephant cutting [sin and merit]{papa-punya}, the two nooses of saṃsāra, and crushing the [pillar]{khambha} of ignorance (cp.16.m4). The sky's [ṭākali]{takali} he explains as being driven on by the unstruck sound, by which the mind-elephant goes to the lake of nirvāṇa. He leaves the chain unexplained.

equations.en: being driven on by the unstruck sound

citations.work: a song or dohā of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), cited by its opening words only; not identified

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'he clearly teaches reality' (de kho na nyid gsal bar gsungs) for 'he brings out that same meaning' (tam evārthaṃ dyotayati); 'in order to stop' ('gog pa'i phyir) for 'cutting' (khaṇḍayitvā); 'destroying' ('joms pa) for 'crushing'; 'the lake-grove of nirvāṇa' (mya ngan las 'das pa'i mtsho'i tshal); and 'in the sky, ṭa ge' (nam mkhar Ta ge) for gaganaṭaka.
gaganaṭaka is Munidatta's form of the song's gaaṇa ṭākali, without the final -li. He explains it only by what it does (driving the mind-elephant on), so the literal sense of ṭākali remains open.
The song twists the chain (sikala) at the pillar's place; Munidatta does not mention the chain, and makes sin and merit themselves the two nooses. His dvau, 'the two', stands for the song's beṇi.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena svacittasyādvaidhīkāratām āha —
mahārasetyādi | bhāvābhāvayor aikyaṃ mahāsukharasaṃ tena pānena pramattaḥ san tribhuvanasya grahopekṣāṃ karoti | bhāvābhāvagrāhyādivikalpaṃ karoti | ata eva pañcaviṣayāṇāṃ nāyakatvena sa eva ṣaṣṭho mahāvajradharaḥ | punaḥ kleśaṃ vipakṣakāriṇan na paśyati |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks of making his own [mind]{citta} nondual: '[Great essence]{maharasa}…' and so on. The oneness of [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava} is the juice of [great bliss]{mahasukha}; [drunk]{matta} by drinking it, he disregards grasping at the [three worlds]{trailokya}. He forms [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of being and nonbeing, of the grasped and the rest. For this very reason, as [leader]{nayaka} of the five [sense objects]{visaya}, he himself is the sixth, the great [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}. Further, he does not see [affliction]{klesa} acting as an [adversary]{vipaksa}.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the great essence as the juice of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the oneness of being and nonbeing; drunk on it, he disregards grasping at the three worlds (cp.16.m5). As leader of the five sense objects he is the sixth, great [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}, and sees no opposing affliction. Where the Sanskrit says he forms concepts, the Tibetan negates it.

equations.en: the juice of great bliss (mahāsukharasa), the oneness of being and nonbeing
he himself, the sixth, the great Vajradhara

flags.note: The printed sentence bhāvābhāvagrāhyādivikalpaṃ karoti, 'he forms conceptual thought of being and nonbeing, of the grasped and the rest', contradicts its context: he has just disregarded grasping, and the next sentence begins 'for this very reason' he is Vajradhara. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has a negative: 'one does not form conceptual thought (rnam par rtog pa mi bya'o) about the grasped of the oneness of being and nonbeing'. A na has probably dropped out (vikalpaṃ na karoti). I translate the Sanskrit as printed; see questions.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) lacks everything from 'is the juice of great bliss' to 'disregards grasping at the three worlds' (mahāsukharasaṃ … grahopekṣāṃ karoti): it runs 'the oneness of being and nonbeing' straight on to 'the grasped' (dngos po dang dngos po med pa dag gcig pa'i gzung ba la). This looks like an eye-skip from the first bhāvābhāva to the second, in the translation or in its manuscript.
The Tibetan introduction reads 'he teaches it as nondual with his own mind' (rang gi sems dang gnyis su med par gsungs) for 'he speaks of making his own mind nondual' (svacittasyādvaidhīkāratām āha).

grahopekṣā, 'disregard of grasping', picks up the song's uekhī, 'disregarding'; tribhuvanasya may be the object of the grasping (as translated) or of the disregard. punaḥ may mean 'further' or 'any longer'.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena nirvvikalpaṃ pratipādayati —
khararavītyādi | mahāsukharāgānalena preritaḥ san sa eva cittagajendraḥ gaganagaṅgā mahāsukhacakraśarovaraṃ gatvā militaḥ | siddhācāryyo hi mahīdharaḥ evaṃ vadati | asmin magne sati mayā 'sya svarūpaṃ kim api na dṛṣṭaṃ nirvvikalpaṃ |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
iti tāvat mṛṣā sarvvaṃ yāvat yāvat vikalpyate
tat satyaṃ tad yathābhūtaṃ tattva[ṃ] yan na vikalpyate || 16 ||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he teaches what is free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}: 'Harsh [sun]{surya}…' and so on. Driven on by the fire of the [passion]{raga-passion} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, that same [mind]{citta}, lord of [elephants]{elephant}, went to the [sky-Gaṅgā]{gagana-ganga}, the [lake]{lake} of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, and merged. The [siddha]{siddha} master [Mahīdhara]{p-mahidhara} speaks thus: 'Sunk in this, I saw nothing at all of its [true nature]{svarupa}: it is free of conceptual thought.' And so the [scripture]{agama}: 'Everything is false just so far as it is conceptualized; what is not conceptualized is true, is as it really is, is [reality]{tattva}.'
segments.note: Munidatta's paraphrase has the fire of the passion of [great bliss]{mahasukha} for the harsh sun's heat, and the [sky-Gaṅgā]{gagana-ganga}, the lake of the wheel of great bliss, for the courtyard of the sky: there the mind-elephant goes and merges (cp.16.m6). Sunk in it, Mahīdhara sees nothing of its nature, which is free of concepts.

equations.en: the lake of the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakrasarovara)

citations.quoted: iti tāvat mṛṣā sarvvaṃ yāvat yāvat vikalpyate | tat satyaṃ tad yathābhūtaṃ tattvaṃ yan na vikalpyate
citations.work: unidentified; Munidatta introduces it only as 'the scripture' (āgama)

flags.note: gaganagaṅgā stands in the nominative, outside the construction with mahāsukhacakraśarovaraṃ. It may be a corruption of gaganāṅgaṇa, the song's 'courtyard of the sky' (gaaṇāṅgaṇa, 5a), a difference of a letter or two in Bengali script. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no Gaṅgā: it has the mind-elephant 'circling in the sky' (nam mkhar 'khor ba), and its line renders the courtyard of the sky nam mkha'i 'khor sa, so its manuscript may have read āṅgaṇa. I translate as printed; see questions.
śarovara (শরোবর) is a spelling of sarovara, 'lake', as in nirvvāṇasarovaraṃ (cp.16.m4).

asmin magne sati could be a locative absolute, 'when this [the mind-elephant] had sunk', or 'sunk in this'; I follow the song ('sinking here') and the Tibetan ('di la byin pa ni, 'sunk in this'). nirvikalpaṃ may qualify 'its true nature' or sum up ('it is free of conceptual thought'); the Tibetan takes it as a summary (rnam par mi rtog pa'o).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'attains' (thob pa) for 'merged' (militaḥ), and 'spoke suchness' (de bzhin nyid gsungs) for 'speaks thus' (evaṃ vadati). In the verse it has 'truth itself becomes thus; reality itself is nonconceptual' (bden pa de nyid de bzhin 'gyur/ de nyid rnam par mi rtog pa). The verse as printed opens with iti, which seems out of place; I leave it untranslated.

questions: cp.16.2a: the refrain's cīagaandā is cīa ('mind') plus gaanda ('lord of elephants'). Munidatta's cittagajendra (cp.16.m1, cp.16.m3) and the Tibetan line (sems nyid … glang chen dbang po) both keep 'mind', but the draft has only 'The drunk elephant runs', perhaps because the elephant entry forbids 'mind' inside a verse line. Here 'mind' is the poet's own word, not a reading. Should the line say 'mind-elephant'?

cp.16.1a: the draft has the unstruck sound roar. Munidatta (cp.16.m2) has the mind-elephant roar on hearing it, and the Tibetan line has an elephant roaring (rab 'jigs glang chen sgrogs) where the Bengali has ghaṇa. Keep the draft and note the divergence, or flag the line?

cp.16.m5: the printed Sanskrit says he forms concepts of being and nonbeing and of the grasped; the Tibetan has a negative, which the context needs. I translated the print and flagged it high. Would you rather emend to 'does not form' in the translation?

cp.16.m6: gaganagaṅgā may be a corruption of the song's gaganāṅgaṇa, 'courtyard of the sky'; the Tibetan comment has no Gaṅgā. If so, the proposed entry gagana-ganga rests on a scribal error. Keep it, or mark it doubtful?

cp.16.m2: the Guhyasamāja passage is odd as printed (pratyāhāra, 'withdrawal'); the Tibetan points to a crosswise text with pravyāhāra, 'utterance'. It is worth checking against an edition of the tantra, which I could not do.
cp.16.m1: for Shastri's tamekārtha I read 'that same meaning' (tam evārthaṃ, as in cp.16.m4); the Tibetan's 'meaning of reality' probably renders the same words. Agree?

Names: I link Munidatta's own forms, Mahīdhara and Kṛṣṇācārya, to p-mahidhara and p-kanha, as the draft links the song's Mahittā. Would you prefer the approved Mahīdharapāda and Kāṇha inside the commentary?

cp.16.2b: Munidatta has the elephant churn 'the conceptual thought of moon and sun, of day and night' (cp.16.m3), and the Tibetan line has sun and moon circling in the sky (nyi zla 'khor). The draft's 'churns the edge of the sky in delight' follows the Bengali; does tusem̐ deserve a line flag?
